title: Microsoft.Extensions.Options
description: A library for configuring and accessing strongly-typed options in .NET applications.

data.text: The Options pattern replaces magic strings and `IConfiguration["Some:Key"]` lookups with strongly-typed classes. You bind a configuration section to a POCO once, and consumers depend on that POCO instead of on the configuration system. This makes settings discoverable, testable, and validatable.

`Microsoft.Extensions.Options` is part of the shared framework for ASP.NET Core and the generic host. In a plain console app you can install it as a package; the JSON binder lives in `Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Binder`.

data.title: Install for a console app
data.content: ASP.NET Core apps already reference these; console apps need them explicitly.
data.code:
dotnet add package Microsoft.Extensions.Options
dotnet add package Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Json
dotnet add package Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Binder

data.title: Bind a section and consume it
data.content: Register the options class, then inject the right interface for the scenario.

terms.definition: Singleton access to the configured value. Use it when the value never changes at runtime.
Scoped access that re-reads configuration per request, so changed appsettings are picked up (or the value reloads when passed as a parameter).
Singleton that supports change notifications via OnChange and is safe to use in long-lived services.
Runs validation during application startup so a bad configuration fails the deploy instead of the first request.

data.title: Interview answer
data.text: The classic trap is resolving `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` inside a singleton: snapshot is scoped, so injecting it into a singleton throws at runtime. Use `IOptionsMonitor<T>` in singletons, and enable `ValidateOnStart` so misconfiguration is caught before traffic arrives.

The Options pattern turns raw configuration keys into a typed class. Instead of reading `Configuration["Smtp:Host"]` as a string at each call site, you bind a section to a class once and inject `IOptions<T>` where it is needed. That removes magic strings and puts the shape of the settings in one place.

data.title: A typed options class with validation
IOptions vs IOptionsSnapshot vs IOptionsMonitor
data.text: `IOptions<T>` is a singleton and never changes after start. `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` is scoped and re-reads the section once per request, which suits settings that change without a restart. `IOptionsMonitor<T>` is a singleton that reacts to changes through `OnChange`. Choosing the right one is the distinction interviewers probe.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Options bind configuration sections to strongly-typed classes
IOptions is singleton, IOptionsSnapshot is scoped, IOptionsMonitor supports change notifications
ValidateDataAnnotations + ValidateOnStart catch bad configuration at startup
Named options (`Configure<T>(name, ...)`) support multiple configurations of the same type
data.takeaway: Use the Options pattern whenever a service needs settings, and validate them once at startup.
